system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 11 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 60-85 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2185-11-02 21:05:00 to 2185-11-13 18:10:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of type II diabetes, morbid obesity, atrial fibrillation, and prior strokes was admitted for evaluation of rapidly spreading blisters and redness on the left foot. Dermatology diagnosed bullous diabeticorum, and the patient received IV antibiotics as a precaution. A minor procedure was performed to drain a large blister. Despite medical advice to stay overnight, the patient left against medical advice the evening of admission. He was discharged on his home medications with instructions to keep the wound dressing clean and dry and to follow up promptly with outpatient care. No oral antibiotics were prescribed at discharge.

as evidenced by leukocytosis, tachycardia. He underwent open 
partial amputation with podiatry. He was started on vancomycin 
and zosyn. He underwent a second debridement and wound vacuum

suggested that the patinet be continued on zosyn with 
discontinuation of vancomycin. They suggested zosyn be switched

Infectious disease will follow him as an outpatient and 
recommended 6 weeks of IV ertapenem.

Pre-operative CXR with evidence of some pulmonary edema ___ the 
setting of known systolic CHF. Low suspicion for pneumonia, but

His oxygen was titrated to room air within 24 hours of 
admission. Patient continued to have hypoxic spells while

insulin by his PCP. He states that he takes 45U Humilin ___ the 
morning. However, he has not always been compliant with this.

His sugars were stable.

initially held given hypotension. Patient started to complain of

need to be restarted as an outpatient.

Brief Hospital Course:
This is a ___ male with PMHx poorly-controlled diabetes, 
systolic CHF, and chronic foot ulcerations followed by podiatry 
presenting with chills and found to have gas gangrene of his

medical floor

ACUTE ISSUES:

# Hypotension
Post-operatively developed hypotension with SBP ___ the ___. 
___ be related to sedation (propofol and midazolam during the 
case) or sepsis (has a leukocytosis) from likely infected right 
hallux. No clear evidence of pneumonia or UTI. No concern for 
biliary sepsis. He was fluid resuscitated with small boluses 
given known systolic heart failure with improvement ___ BP and 
normalization of lactate. He was treated with antibiotics as 
below for infected hallux. Patients pressures improved and were 
stable on the floor.

# Sepsis from Gas Gangrene
Presented with gas gangrene of his first right hallux and sepsis 
as evidenced by leukocytosis, tachycardia. He underwent open 
partial amputation with podiatry. He was started on vancomycin 
and zosyn. He underwent a second debridement and wound vacuum 
placement. Patient was seen by the infectious disease team who 
suggested that the patinet be continued on zosyn with 
discontinuation of vancomycin. They suggested zosyn be switched 
to ertapenem on discharge. PICC was placed during hospital stay. 
Infectious disease will follow him as an outpatient and 
recommended 6 weeks of IV ertapenem.  

# Hypoxemia
Post-operatively had hypoxemia with a 5L NC requirement. 
Pre-operative CXR with evidence of some pulmonary edema ___ the 
setting of known systolic CHF. Low suspicion for pneumonia, but 
this is a possibility given leukocytosis. Unlikley PE given lack 
of tachcyardia and INR is supratherapeutic. Was notably more 
hypoxic when sleeping; does have known OSA but declines CPAP. 
His oxygen was titrated to room air within 24 hours of 
admission. Patient continued to have hypoxic spells while 
sleeping be declined any supplemental oxygen. He complained of 
orthopnea that was likely secondary to his systolic heart 
failure, immobility and holding of his blood pressure 
medications.  

# Hyperbilirubinemia
Presented with new elevated total bilirubin. Has no RUQ pain, no 
clear evidence of hemolysis. Has prior hepatitis serologies ___

Anticoagulated on warfarin for atrial fibrillation. Presented 
with INR elevated to 7.2 on admission peaked at 9, most recently

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mr. ___ . I'm Dr. ___ , one of your hospital doctors. You came in tonight with chills and some concerns about your foot. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve been feeling off for a few days. I had chills, and my skin looks kind of orange now. And I’ve been short of breath, especially when I lie down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And your foot — you had some ulcers before, correct? What happened recently?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I go to the podiatrist for ulcers on both feet. I missed my last appointment, but went back a few days ago. They cleaned out the right big toe — it was really bad. Since then, I started feeling worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That lines up. The X-ray showed gas in the soft tissue of your right toe — that’s a sign of a serious infection called gas gangrene. You were taken to surgery tonight to remove the toe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: They amputated it? I didn’t know it was that bad…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was necessary to stop the infection from spreading. After surgery, your blood pressure dropped, so we brought you to the ICU for close monitoring. You’re stable now, but we’re watching you carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t feel any pain. But I was cold and shaky. Is that from the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The chills and low blood pressure are signs of sepsis — your body’s response to a severe infection. Your white blood cell count was high, and your lactate was elevated, which confirms that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Sepsis? That sounds dangerous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It is serious, but we caught it early. You’re on strong antibiotics — vancomycin and piperacillin-tazobactam — to fight the infection. We’ll adjust based on culture results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… what about my breathing? I still feel winded.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray shows some fluid in the lungs — likely from your heart failure. You were on oxygen after surgery, but your levels improved. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have heart failure… and diabetes. My sugars are always high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your A1C is 8.1%, so your diabetes is not well controlled. That makes infections harder to heal. We’ve restarted your insulin — 30 units with meals plus sliding scale — and your sugars are better now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t been consistent with my insulin. I forget sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand, but for your foot to heal, keeping your blood sugar in check is critical. We’ll work with you on that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from last night show your bilirubin is high — that’s why your skin looks orange. It’s likely due to the infection affecting your liver, not a liver disease.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it serious? Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s concerning, but not unexpected with sepsis. Your ultrasound showed a slightly thickened gallbladder, but no stones or infection. Your liver numbers are starting to improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing — your INR was very high, over 7. That’s because of your warfarin. You’re at risk for bleeding, so we gave a small dose of vitamin K and held the warfarin for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had high INRs before. I guess I need to get it checked more often.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially with infections and antibiotics. We’ve started enoxaparin to bridge you until your INR is safer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your wound is healing, but we noticed more dead tissue during a check. We’ll need to go back to the OR tomorrow for another debridement — cleaning out any remaining infected tissue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another surgery? How many times will this happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We hope this is the last time. It’s important to remove all infected tissue so the antibiotics can work. After that, we’ll place a wound vacuum to help it heal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, whatever it takes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did well in surgery. We cleaned out the area and placed the wound vac. It will help draw out fluid and promote healing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It feels tight. Is that normal?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s the suction working. The nurse will check it regularly. We also got your culture back — it grew Staph aureus, which is treatable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that what caused the infection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, methicillin-sensitive Staph aureus. Good news — it’s not MRSA. The infectious disease team recommends switching from vancomycin to ertapenem for six weeks via IV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Six weeks of IV antibiotics? Where will I get those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll place a PICC line — a long IV in your arm — so you can get antibiotics at an extended care facility. Infectious disease will follow you closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your PICC line was placed successfully. You’ll start ertapenem tomorrow. How’s your breathing and swelling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still short of breath when I lie flat. My legs are more swollen too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s from your heart failure. We held your diuretic because of low blood pressure, but now that you’re stable, we’re restarting torsemide 40mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I usually take it when my legs swell. Should I keep taking it at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but we’re holding your ramipril and spironolactone for now. Once your kidney function and blood pressure stay stable, you can restart them as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You mentioned wrist pain. Any injury?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, but the IV site has been sore. I think it leaked a bit.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The X-ray shows no fracture. It’s likely swelling from IV infiltration. Keep it elevated, and it should improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is down to normal, and your kidney function is stable. That’s great progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m getting better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. The infection is responding. You’re on day 3 of IV ertapenem, and your wound looks clean. We’ll keep the wound vac for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your INR is now 2.4 — safe to restart warfarin. We’ll adjust the dose and check it regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need to get blood tests after I leave?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, weekly at first. Also, weekly blood tests for infection markers — ESR and CRP — to make sure the osteomyelitis is clearing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. The plan is to transfer you to an extended care facility tomorrow for the rest of your IV antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not home yet?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. You need six weeks of IV antibiotics and wound care. The facility is equipped for that. Your podiatrist and infectious disease will follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check before transfer. Your vitals are stable, lungs are clearer, and wound is healing. Any questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be able to walk normally?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll need a special shoe and possibly physical therapy. With good diabetes control, you can prevent further foot problems.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll try to stick to my insulin this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That will make a big difference. Also, keep your follow-up appointments — especially for your INR and foot checks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick visit before discharge. Your labs are stable, and you’re ready for transfer tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, doctor. I didn’t think I’d make it through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve come a long way. Keep up the good work with your health — it’s worth it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Today’s the day. You’re being discharged to extended care. Remember: continue IV ertapenem, take torsemide, hold ramipril and spironolactone, and monitor your blood sugar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And get my INR checked weekly?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. And weekly blood tests for infection. Your care team will coordinate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll do my best. Thanks for everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of type II diabetes, morbid obesity, atrial fibrillation, and chronic foot ulcers was admitted with chills and found to have gas gangrene of the right first toe. He underwent amputation and a subsequent debridement with wound vac placement. His postoperative course was complicated by sepsis, hypotension, and acute kidney injury, requiring ICU monitoring. He was treated with IV antibiotics, later transitioned to ertapenem via PICC line for six weeks. His heart failure was managed with diuresis, and his warfarin was adjusted after an elevated INR. He was stabilized and discharged to an extended care facility for ongoing IV antibiotic therapy and wound care.
problems: Acute on chronic systolic heart failure
Diabetes with peripheral circulatory disorders, type II or unspecified type, uncontrolled
Ulcer of other part of foot
Personal history of noncompliance with medical treatment, presenting hazards to health
